title: The forty tradition
hook: scholars gathered forty hadith, hoping for a reward promised in a report

segments.voice: Yesterday, weak hadith and virtue, and your line: careful with the weak. Did you catch a quote before you passed it on? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

Here is a book that begins by admitting something. In the introduction to his little collection of forty hadith, the scholar al-Nawawi mentions a report: whoever preserves forty hadith about the religion for the Prophet's community will be raised among the people of knowledge. He says that promise is what moved scholars before him to gather forties of their own. And right there, in his own introduction, al-Nawawi says the report is weak. Yesterday's question, sitting on the first pages of a real book. So why write it at all? Today: the forty tradition.
screen: `A BOOK THAT ADMITS SOMETHING.` → `PRESERVE FORTY.` → `AND THE REPORT IS WEAK.`

segments.voice: Start with the hope. The report promises that someone who preserves forty hadith for the community, on matters of the religion, will be raised with the scholars. Al-Nawawi notes that it comes by many routes and that the hadith critics agree it is weak. He also names scholars before him who gathered forties anyway, on belief, on law, on renouncing the world, on good manners, each with a different aim. Then look at his own footing. He doesn't rest the book on the weak report. He points instead to sound ones: the Prophet's instruction that whoever is present should pass his words on to whoever is absent, and the prayer for the one who hears his words and conveys them as he heard them. That's the prayer from the day on memorizing chains, now holding up a whole book. Next, what he chose to gather. Not forty on a single subject. He gathered sayings he considered foundations, each one, as he described it, a great principle of the religion. His collection opens with the report on intentions, the line that also opens Bukhari's Sahih. The second is the hadith of Jibril: Islam, iman and ihsan, met last week. And the line memorized two days back, religion is sincere counsel, has its place in it too. Last, why forty. The book never claims the number is holy. It's a number a person can carry. A forty is a book built to fit inside a memory, and that's how it's used: learned, recited, taught line by line, small enough to take anywhere and deep enough to keep opening.
screen: `THE HOPE IN A WEAK REPORT.` · `HIS FOOTING: SOUND REPORTS.` · `FORTY FOUNDATIONS, NOT ONE TOPIC.` · `A BOOK THAT FITS IN A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at al-Nawawi's forty. Later today, if you can, open it and read just the headings of the first few. For now, take its first two, both already met on this path. Actions are only by intentions. Islam, iman, ihsan. Say them in order, as the collection does, one on each slow breath. Then let one question sit with you: if you could carry forty sayings anywhere, which one would you want in your pocket first? Don't answer quickly. Just let the question rest. The bell holds the time.
The forty tradition. Collections of forty hadith, gathered in hope of a promise from a weak report, and grounded by al-Nawawi on sound reports about passing the Prophet's words on. Today's word.

Your line: forty to carry. Today, add a third short saying to those two, religion is sincere counsel or another from al-Nawawi's forty, and say all three before bed. Tomorrow: hadith commentary. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim students learn and memorize al-Nawawi's forty, line by line with a teacher, and other scholars have compiled forties of their own on many subjects.

fork.setup: you're al-Nawawi. the report that inspired forty-hadith collections is weak. what do you do?
options: drop the whole idea of a forty.
write the forty, say plainly the report is weak, and rest the book on sound reports.
call the report sound, so no one doubts the book.
fork.reveal: he writes it, names the weakness himself, and grounds his work on sound reports about passing the Prophet's words on.

original.note: Arabic: the forty, the name given to this kind of collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: forty must be a holy number in hadith.
what it means: a report promised a reward for preserving forty, and scholars gathered forties in hope.
what a scholar hears: al-Nawawi calls that report weak in his own introduction and stands his book on sound reports about conveying.

notes: Al-Nawawi's introduction: confirm that he (a) cites the 'whoever preserves forty hadith' report, (b) says it comes by many routes and that the huffaz agree it is weak, (c) names earlier compilers of forties on varied subjects (summarized here as belief, law, worship, good manners), (d) rests his work on 'let the one present convey to the one absent' and 'may Allah brighten the face...', and (e) calls each chosen hadith a great principle (qa'ida 'azima) of the religion.

Al-Nawawi's introduction also states that scholars agree on acting on weak hadith in fada'il; this was left out to stay consistent with day 1163, which presents the matter as disputed. A Keeper may want to reconcile.
The number of hadith in al-Nawawi's collection is not stated (it is commonly said to contain more than forty); only 'forty' as the genre name is used.
Bukhari 67 for 'let the one present convey to the one absent' (Farewell Sermon); confirm number (also Bukhari 105, 1741).

Editor: 'the reason' for earlier forties now attributed to al-Nawawi ('he says'); his list of earlier forties changed from 'worship' to 'renouncing the world' (zuhd) in teach and myth; references to the line memorized on 1162 updated to its new hadith (Muslim 55, religion is sincere counsel, al-Nawawi's no. 7); practice and carry reworded to match.
